segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show his slaves what must soon take place. He made it known by sending his angel to his slave John,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who testified to the word of God and to the testimony of Jesus Christ, to everything he saw.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of the prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and keep what is written in it, for the time is near.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: John, to the seven assemblies in Asia: Grace to you and peace from the one who is and who was and who is coming, and from the seven spirits who are before his throne,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and from Jesus Christ, the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of the kings of the earth. To him who loves us and freed us from our sins by his blood,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father—to him be the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look, he is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him. Yes, amen.

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “I am the Alpha and the Omega,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: says the Lord God,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “the one who is and who was and who is coming, the Almighty.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I, John, your brother and partner in the affliction and kingdom and endurance that are in Jesus, was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I was in the Spirit on the Lord’s day, and I heard behind me a loud voice like a trumpet,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Write what you see in a scroll and send it to the seven assemblies: to Ephesus and to Smyrna and to Pergamum and to Thyatira and to Sardis and to Philadelphia and to Laodicea.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I turned to see the voice that was speaking with me, and when I turned I saw seven golden lampstands,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and among the lampstands one like a son of man, clothed in a robe reaching to his feet and with a golden sash wrapped around his chest.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: His head and his hair were white like white wool, like snow, and his eyes were like a flame of fire,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: his feet were like fine bronze, as if fired in a furnace, and his voice was like the sound of many waters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In his right hand he held seven stars, and from his mouth came a sharp two-edged sword, and his face was like the sun shining in its strength.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When I saw him, I fell at his feet as though dead. And he placed his right hand on me, saying,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do not be afraid. I am the first and the last,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and the living one—I was dead, and look, I am alive forever and ever—and I have the keys of death and of Hades.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So write what you have seen, and what is, and what is going to take place after this.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: As for the secret meaning of the seven stars that you saw in my right hand, and of the seven golden lampstands: the seven stars are the angels of the seven assemblies, and the seven lampstands are the seven assemblies.”

notes.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and a first-century reader would have heard it that way. Most English versions use “servants,” partly because the Septuagint uses the word for the prophets as God’s devoted agents and partly because “slave” carries the weight of modern history. The term here expresses belonging and obedience, not degradation.
The Greek phrase can mean “soon” or “quickly,” that is, swiftly once it begins. Most translators choose “soon,” supported by “the time is near” in verse 3. The other reading is possible.

The contrast between one reader and many hearers shows that public reading is meant. Few people owned or could read books, so a document like this was read aloud to the gathered community by one person.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people: a city’s citizen assembly, or in the Greek Old Testament, Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and is not wrong, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so the reader sees the same word each time.
This is the Roman province of Asia, the western part of modern Turkey, not the continent. All seven cities named in verse 11 lay within it.

notes.phrase: the one who is and who was and who is coming
notes.traditional: him which is, and which was, and which is to come
notes.note: The Greek deliberately breaks normal grammar here, leaving the title in an unchanged form after “from,” as if it were a name that cannot be altered. “The one who is” echoes the Greek version of God’s self-naming to Moses in Exodus 3:14. The third element is literally “the coming one,” not “the one who will be.”

Many interpreters take this as a symbolic way of naming the Holy Spirit in fullness, since the phrase stands between God and Jesus Christ in a blessing. Others take the seven spirits to be seven chief angels before God’s throne, a figure known from Jewish writings. The translation keeps the literal wording and leaves the question open.

The earliest and best manuscripts read “freed” (or “loosed”) us from our sins. Many later manuscripts read “washed,” a Greek word differing by one letter and pronounced almost identically, and this is what the King James Version follows. Nearly all modern editions and translations read “freed.”

notes.phrase: he is coming with the clouds
notes.note: The verse weaves together two Old Testament passages: Daniel 7:13, where one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven, and Zechariah 12:10, where people look on the one they pierced and mourn. “All the tribes of the earth” could also be read as “all the tribes of the land,” as in Zechariah, but Revelation’s scope here appears to be universal.

The Greek is an ordinary word for hardship or oppression that bears down on people. “Tribulation” is the traditional rendering in Revelation, but many readers now hear it as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the word itself does. John speaks of it as something he and his readers already share.

This is the earliest occurrence of the phrase. Most scholars take it to mean the first day of the week, Sunday, on which Christians met; that usage is clear in Christian writings soon afterward. A minority take it as the prophetic “day of the Lord,” but the Greek wording differs from the usual expression for that.

The word means a written document, which in this period was normally a roll of papyrus. “Book” is the traditional rendering, but it suggests a bound volume with pages, which a first-century reader would not have pictured.

notes.phrase: one like a son of man
notes.traditional: one like unto the Son of man
notes.note: The Greek has no article and echoes Daniel 7:13, where “one like a son of man” means a figure of human appearance. Some translations capitalize the phrase as the title Jesus uses for himself in the Gospels. The figure is clearly the risen Jesus, but the wording here describes what John saw and is left as a description.

This Greek word is found only in Revelation (here and 2:18), and its exact meaning is unknown. It evidently names a gleaming metal or alloy of the copper family; “burnished bronze” and “fine bronze” are the usual guesses. The grammar of the following phrase is also irregular, but the picture of metal glowing in a furnace is clear.

The Greek word means a secret, here the hidden significance of a symbol that is then explained. Most English versions keep “mystery,” treating it as an established term. That word now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, whereas here the meaning is stated plainly at once.

The Greek word means “messenger” and is used of both heavenly and human messengers. Elsewhere in Revelation it always refers to heavenly beings, so most scholars understand heavenly representatives or guardians of each assembly. Others take it as human messengers or leaders of the assemblies; the question remains disputed.

candidates.reason: Occurs throughout the New Testament and translators split between “slave” and “servant,” including in the phrase “slaves of God/Christ”; readers would be misled by variation.
Recurs across Paul, Hebrews, James and Revelation with versions varying among “patience,” “perseverance,” “steadfastness” and “endurance.”
The witness/testimony word group (with μάρτυς and μαρτυρέω) is thematic in John and Revelation and needs one consistent set of English renderings, including whether μάρτυς is ever “martyr.”
Recurs in Revelation, the Gospels and letters, where versions alternate between “book” and “scroll”; a single policy is needed, especially for “book of life.”
Usually “angel” but sometimes a human “messenger”; the choice in Revelation 1–3 and elsewhere should be governed by one stated rule.
